subject: European History
title: 3. Nationalism, Liberalism, Romanticism, Socialism, Industrialization and Colonialism

segments.text: This topic asks candidates to use ideologies as tools for explaining actual political events, not to write abstract definitions in isolation — every definition here should be immediately connected to a historical example of its political effect.

generally defended constitutional government, civil rights, and legal equality against arbitrary rule, though many early liberals supported property-based suffrage rather than universal voting rights.

blocks.text: Industrialization and the Revolutions of 1820, 1830 and 1848

segments.text: Factories, railways, urbanisation and new class structures transformed European society, with a growing bourgeoisie and urban working class generating new political demands and organisations. The revolutions of

mixed constitutional, national and social demands together; most failed in the short term, but they weakened old political assumptions and prepared the later national unification and political reform covered in subsequent topics — 1848 in particular should be studied as a moment where several ideologies met an economic and social crisis simultaneously, not simply as a failure.

European industrial and military power expanded overseas during this period, driven by economic interest, strategic rivalry, missionary activity, nationalism, and ideas of racial hierarchy together — never one single motive alone.

items.text: Constitutional, rights-based political thought, often paired with restricted rather than universal suffrage.
The pan-European upheavals combining constitutional, national and social demands, largely defeated in the short term but significant for later political development.
Prepare each ideology in four lines: core idea, social base, major thinkers/movements, political effect; use 1848 as a case study where several ideologies met economic and social crisis at once.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “How could nationalism function as both a liberal and a conservative or exclusionary force in different nineteenth-century contexts?”
Do not assume nationalism was always liberal; it could also become conservative, imperial or exclusionary.
Do not treat socialism as one doctrine; Marxists, social democrats and other socialists differed sharply.
Do not study 1848 only as a failure; its longer-term effects on nationalism, constitutionalism and political organisation were substantial.
Liberalism emphasised constitutional limits and representative institutions, though often with restricted suffrage.
Nationalism sought political unity or independence and became crucial in Italy, Germany, Poland and the Balkans.
Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto in 1848.
The revolutions of 1848 spread across much of Europe with mixed immediate results but substantial long-term significance.
Never write ideological definitions without immediately showing how those ideas changed actual political events — this is the topic’s central and most frequently tested skill.
Treat nationalism as context-dependent (liberal in some settings, exclusionary in others) rather than as one fixed political tendency.
